macro: The newsletter covers geopolitical developments around the US-Ukraine-Russia conflict, with Washington threatening to withhold intelligence from Kyiv over missile strikes on Russian refineries, and Trump reportedly striking a diesel deal with Putin. Risk tone is mixed as geopolitical uncertainty persists alongside some tentatively improving signals on the Treasury front. Overnight action is shaped by a combination of diplomacy headlines and bond market dynamics.
rates_fed: Treasury selling at the long end of the curve is showing signs of fatigue, and if CPI and PPI this week come in without major upside surprises, a multi-day rally in bonds is possible. A series of supportive data points have accumulated — weak August JOLTs and PCE, soft July payrolls, Fed officials downplaying the need for consecutive hikes, and a slowdown in AI-linked debt issuance. Treasury Secretary Bessent is expected to reduce auction sizes for the 20- and 30-year bonds at the November 4th refunding announcement and shift more issuance toward bills, which would further relieve upward pressure on yields.
market_outlook: Adam's lean is cautiously constructive on rates and by extension equities, contingent on this week's CPI and PPI not coming in hot. The key catalyst to watch is inflation data — a benign print could trigger a meaningful Treasury rally that spills over positively into risk assets. Geopolitical noise around Ukraine-Russia adds an overlay of uncertainty but is not the dominant market driver today.
bull_case: The accumulation of softer macro data points — weak JOLTs, PCE, and NFPs — combined with Fed officials backing away from consecutive hikes creates a favorable backdrop for bonds and equities. A reduction in AI-linked debt issuance removes a source of upward yield pressure that has weighed on markets. Bessent's likely move to trim long-end auction sizes at the November refunding is a structural positive for Treasuries. If CPI and PPI this week are benign, a sustained bond rally could provide a meaningful tailwind for stocks.
bear_case: Geopolitical risk remains elevated with the US-Ukraine-Russia situation fluid and unpredictable, creating headline risk at any moment. The sharp drop in AI-linked borrowing in September could signal market indigestion that potentially slows the pace of data center spending — a headwind for the AI infrastructure trade. Treasury yields remain elevated and any upside inflation surprise this week could reignite selling at the long end. The diplomatic uncertainty between the US, Ukraine, and Russia adds a layer of risk that is difficult to price.

company_items.summary: Meta held talks with Anthropic about potentially selling compute capacity to the AI startup but ultimately decided against it, at least for now. This suggests Meta is evaluating how to monetize or deploy its AI infrastructure assets but has not yet committed to a third-party compute strategy. The decision to pass keeps Meta's compute focused internally for now, with the door left open for future deals.

T-Mobile's CTO John Saw published a LinkedIn piece pushing back on fears that Starlink Mobile poses a major near-term threat to legacy US wireless carriers. Saw argued that the Grain spectrum transaction involves roughly 14 MHz of spectrum T-Mobile previously divested because it was no longer central to its strategy, and that over 70% of mobile traffic occurs indoors where terrestrial networks have a fundamental advantage. The commentary is an attempt to reassure investors that the competitive moat of traditional wireless infrastructure remains intact.

sectors: AI infrastructure and data center spending faces a potential headwind as AI-linked debt issuance fell sharply in September, signaling market indigestion from heavy supply. This could slow the pace of capital deployment into data centers. Legacy US wireless carriers, particularly T-Mobile, are defending their competitive positioning against Starlink Mobile. Treasury and bond markets are the key sector focus this week ahead of CPI and PPI.

tts_summary: Here's what you need to know this morning. The big macro story is in the Treasury market, and it's actually starting to look a bit more constructive. The selling pressure at the long end of the curve is showing signs of exhaustion, and there's a credible argument that if we get a benign CPI and PPI print this week, we could see a bond rally that actually has some legs — more than just the usual one or two day bounce. Think about what's accumulated on the dovish side: weak August job openings, soft PCE, a disappointing July payrolls number, Fed officials stepping back from the idea of consecutive rate hikes, and now a sharp slowdown in AI-linked debt issuance that had been flooding the market with supply. On top of that, Treasury Secretary Bessent is widely expected to trim auction sizes for the 20- and 30-year bonds at the November fourth refunding announcement and redirect more issuance toward bills. That's a structural positive for yields. So the setup heading into this week's inflation data is more hopeful than it's been in a while — but execution matters, and a hot number would unwind that quickly. On the geopolitical front, things remain fluid around Ukraine and Russia. Washington is reportedly threatening to withhold critical intelligence from Kyiv unless it backs off missile and drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Trump is said to have struck a diesel deal with Putin after Zelensky refused to stop those strikes. This is headline risk that could flare at any moment, so keep that in your peripheral vision. On the company side, two names worth noting. First, Meta held talks with Anthropic about selling compute capacity to the AI startup but ultimately passed — for now. It signals Meta is thinking about how to monetize its AI infrastructure externally but hasn't pulled the trigger. Mixed read. Second, T-Mobile's chief technology officer went on the offensive against Starlink Mobile fears, publishing a detailed rebuttal arguing that spectrum ownership alone doesn't make a network. He pointed out that the spectrum involved in the Grain transaction was spectrum T-Mobile had already divested because it wasn't central to their strategy, and that more than seventy percent of mobile traffic happens indoors — where terrestrial networks have a hard structural edge. That's a bullish signal for T-Mobile and the legacy wireless carriers. Net directional read for today: cautiously constructive, with the inflation data as the week's make-or-break catalyst. If we get a clean number, the bond market could finally give equities some room to breathe.
